catalog_quote: Stress in Alorese is marked by higher pitch. If words are uttered in isolation, such as in a wordlist, stress almost always occurs on the penultimate syllable. However, when words are uttered in fast speech, initial syllables can be reduced and the stress moves to another syllable. ... When uttered in isolation, the stress is on the penultimate syllable [ˈla.ra], but when uttered in fast speech, the penultimate vowel becomes schwa as in [lə.ˈra] ... The penultimate syllable is reduced, therefore stress falls on the final syllable. ... When the phonetic schwa occurs in the antepenultimate syllable of a trisyllabic word, the stress remains on the penultimate syllable, even when the word is uttered in fast speech ... In disyllabic words with a final consonant, free variation between penultimate and ultimate stress is observed. An example is tahak 'ripe' which can be pronounced [ˈta.hak] or…

new_statements.quote: Firstly, stress may be an additional phonological factor that could play a role in contact-induced morphological simplification, as exemplified by Kusters (2003) and Molineaux (2012). Stress in Alorese is on the penultimate syllable of the stem (Klamer, 2011: 32–33). Because the suffix is unstressed, and attaches to the ultimate, unstressed, stem syllable, the suffix may be more prone to loss. [p. 25] || Alorese lacks phonemic geminates, while consonant lengthening only occurs in word-medial position as an effect of stress on the penultimate syllable, and when preceded by a vowel that etymologically relates to Proto-Alorese schwa *ə (Klamer, 2011: 30; Sulistyono, 2022: 75). [fn. 5, p. 9]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate; penultimate stress = fixed: penultimate syllable). Adds the domain detail that the penult is counted on the stem and that subject suffixes are unstressed and stress-neutral, plus the stress-conditioned consonant lengthening. The paper is a modelling study, not a phonological description; its stress statement is a citation of Klamer 2011 (A Short Grammar of Alorese, print only, not opened).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the stem; inflectional suffixes are unstressed and do not shift the stress (the domain of the rule is the stem, not the suffixed word). Stated secondhand, citing Klamer 2011: 32-33.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Side detail: phonetic (non-phonemic) consonant lengthening occurs word-medially after the stressed penult when the preceding vowel derives from Proto-Alorese schwa (fn. 5, p. 9); fn. 13 (p. 19) says lengthening of consonants 'is only caused by stress in a list context (Klamer, 2011: 30)'.
new_statements.identity_note: Dekker et al. 2025 does not name a dialect for the stress statement; it treats Alorese as a single language of the Alor and Pantar coasts and takes its phonological facts from Klamer 2011 (A Short Grammar of Alorese), whose variety is not specified in the paper. The Western Lamaholot data used to initialise their model are from the Lewoingu variety (Nishiyama & Kelen 2007), a different language.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage, the domain (compound) sentence and both summary restatements are verbatim in the LOT 614 text we hold at sec. 4.2.4.4 pp. 90-91, 4.2.6 p. 93 and 4.8 p. 141, exactly as the record's locator says. (2) Deciding source: a 2022 Leiden dissertation whose ch. 4 is a fieldwork-based sketch grammar; explicit stress section naming pitch as the cue, penult default, fast-speech reduction to final stress in disyllables, penult retained in trisyllables, free variation in CVC-final disyllables, compound stress on first member. Our the primary-stress rule/the secondary-stress rule/heavy/domain fields track this faithfully. (3) Alternatives: Glottolog has only one other description, Klamer 2011 (Lincom, print-only, not yet obtained); Sulistyono's own citation of Klamer 2011:30 implies it agrees on penultimate stress. Two open items downloaded now (Klamer 2012 LD&C SP5; Sulistyono 2025 Linguistik Indonesia) are silent
